title: Don't Let the Tools Take Over
author: Foster Chance
summary: Cindy of Foster Chance argues that the defining problem of the current moment is not technological disruption itself but the quiet surrender of attention, agency, and self-direction to tools engineered to capture and hold us. Like fish unaware of the water, she writes, we sleepwalk through our lives while a steady stream of alarming images and messages pushes us to react, leaving us with less choice, less growth, and less connection. She draws a sharp line between relying on technology (reaching for a tool when it serves you) and depending on it (letting the tool run the show), and insists that real leadership is irreducibly human, grounded in trust, meaning, and connection that no productivity system can optimize.
points: There is a critical difference between relying on technology and being dependent on it: reliance means reaching for a tool when it serves you, while dependence means the tool is running the show.
Leading yourself is an act of self-respect that comes first; only when you genuinely respect and care for yourself can you extend that same care to the people around you.

Cindy prescribes four grounded practices: build life around restorative recovery experiences, believe you can grow (Carol Dweck's growth mindset), practice self-compassion (Kristin Neff), and return to your values.
Attempts to 'optimize' people treat human beings as machines to be tuned; the author argues we should seek to understand people rather than optimize them.
Used intentionally, technology can protect time and attention and offload low-value tasks, but only when a focused person gives it clear direction from their values.
quotes: Like fish unaware of the water, we live unaware of the opportunity right in front of us — to take responsibility for ourselves, to claim our freedom, to choose what we actually pay attention to.
There is a critical difference between relying on technology and being dependent on it. Reliance means you reach for a tool when it serves you. Dependence means the tool is running the show.
Leadership — real leadership — is human, and it is based on one human trusting and being inspired by another human.
You are a heart, a mind, and a spirit. You are nourished by meaning, values, and vision — not by a better productivity system.

The people thriving right now, in every disrupted industry and every corner of life, are not the ones who surrendered to the tools. They are the ones who doubled down on what makes them irreplaceable as humans: trust, judgment, empathy, genuine connection.
Think of technology as a capable assistant who works best with clear direction from a focused boss.
In a distracted and fragmented world, the trust between human beings is the most valuable currency there is.
